mainTopic: Paying for hidden or unexpected items destroyed by fire or other damage, when the owner's oath is believed, and the difference between a גזלן and a חמסן.
overview: The ברייתא limits the argument between רבי יהודה and the חכמים about hidden items burned in a stack. It applies only when the fire spread from the burner's own land, and it lists cases where even רבי יהודה agrees the burner pays only for what he agreed to or could see. רבא rules that a woman given a gold דינר described as silver pays for gold if she damages it herself, but only for silver if she was careless. רב מרדכי says this rule is already clear from the wheat-and-barley ברייתא. שמואל explains that, according to רבי יהודה, the owner of burned hidden items may swear and collect like a robbery victim (תקנת נגזל). אמימר asks whether the same applies to the victim of a מסור, and the question ends with תיקו. In the case of a safe kicked into a river, a claim of coins is believed, but whether a claim of a pearl is believed stays תיקו. A claim of a silver goblet is believed with an oath only from a wealthy or trusted person. Finally, רב אשי explains that a חמסן pays for what he takes while a גזלן does not, and that a forced sale is valid only when the seller says "רוצה אני."

steps.title: Limiting the argument to a fire that spread from one's own land
steps.stepSummary: The מחלוקת about hidden items applies only when the fire started on the burner's own property. If he lit it on his friend's property, everyone agrees he pays for everything inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: When is this argument said? When someone lit a fire on his own land and it spread and burned on his friend's land. But if he lit the fire right on his friend's land, everyone agrees he pays for everything that was inside the stack.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא is setting a limit on the argument between רבי יהודה and the חכמים about paying for hidden things burned in a stack.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים exempt hidden items only when the fire traveled from the burner's land to his friend's land. If he lit the fire directly on his friend's property, he is responsible for everything there, hidden or not. So the dispute is narrower than it first looked.

keyTerms.meaning: In what case is this said? (a phrase that limits a ruling)
one who kindles or lights a fire

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the חכמים always exempt hidden items. Their exemption applies only when the fire spread from the burner's own land.

phrases.english: In what case are these words said?
phrases.notes: This points back to the argument about paying for the vessels hidden inside the stack that got burned.

phrases.english: When one kindles a fire on his own property
and it spread and burned on his friend's property.
But one who kindles a fire on his friend's property
according to everyone, he pays
for everything that was inside it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from the previous עמוד about רבי יהודה and the חכמים on hidden items.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The exemption for hidden items applies only when the fire spread from the burner's own land. If he lit it on his friend's land, he pays for everything.

steps.title: רבי יהודה agrees about a stack placed in a borrowed spot with hidden items
steps.stepSummary: If someone lent space to stack grain and the borrower also hid items in the stack, even רבי יהודה agrees the field owner pays only for the stack.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה agrees with the חכמים in this case: someone lent space in his field to his friend so the friend could make a stack of grain. The friend made the stack and hid things inside it. Here the field owner pays only for the stack itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a case where even רבי יהודה, who usually makes the burner pay for hidden items, agrees he pays only for the stack.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Permission was given only to stack grain, not to hide valuables inside it. Since the hidden items were never part of what the field owner agreed to, he does not pay for them. רבי יהודה's usual view does not apply here.

keyTerms.meaning: to pile up a stack of grain

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda agrees with the Rabbis
in a case where one lends space to his friend
to pile up a stack of grain,
and he stacked it and hid items inside,
that he pays only
the value of the stack alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After narrowing the חכמים' view, the ברייתא now narrows רבי יהודה's view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When space was lent only for stacking, the owner who burns it pays only for the stack, not for hidden items.

steps.title: Wheat and barley switched or mixed: pay only for barley
steps.stepSummary: If wheat was stacked where barley was agreed, or the reverse, or one grain was covered with the other, the payment is only for barley.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same is true if he got permission to stack wheat and stacked barley, or permission for barley and stacked wheat. It is also true if he stacked wheat and covered it with barley, or stacked barley and covered it with wheat. In all these cases he pays only the value of barley.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds more cases of רבי יהודה's agreement. These are cases where what was stacked is different from what was agreed to or what could be seen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Barley is worth less than wheat. When there is a mismatch between what was agreed, what was seen, and what was really there, the payment goes down to the cheaper grain, barley. The burner never took on responsibility for more valuable wheat.
steps.whatToRemember: Even רבי יהודה agrees that a person pays only for what he agreed to or could see. Anything extra that was hidden or switched is not his responsibility.

phrases.english: Permission to stack wheat, and he stacked barley;
permission for barley, and he stacked wheat;
wheat, and he covered it with barley;
barley, and he covered it with wheat
that he pays only
the value of barley alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more cases to רבי יהודה's agreement from step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In any wheat/barley mismatch, he pays only the lower value of barley.

steps.title: רבא: a gold coin given as silver that she damages herself
steps.stepSummary: If someone gives a woman a gold דינר but tells her it is silver, and she herself damages it, she pays the full gold value.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Someone gave a gold דינר to a woman to watch and told her, 'Be careful with it, it is silver.' If she damaged it herself, she pays for a gold דינר. This is because he can say to her, 'What business did you have damaging it?'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא starts a new rule about watching an item that is worth more than you were told. Here he gives the first half: when the watcher damages it herself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Damaging something with your own hands is not about how well you guarded it. It is harm you did directly. So the real value counts, and it does not matter what she was told.

keyTerms.meaning: what business did you have with it?

phrases.english: Rava said:
One who gives a gold dinar to a woman,
phrases.notes: He gives it to her to watch for him.

phrases.english: and says to her: 'Be careful with it,
it is made of silver';
if she damaged it, she pays a gold dinar,
because he can say to her:
'What business did you have with it, that you damaged it?'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: הַנּוֹתֵן דִּינַר זָהָב לְאִשָּׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new statement whose idea (you are responsible only for what you agreed to) is close to the wheat/barley cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A watcher who damages the item herself pays its real value, even if she was told it was worth less.

steps.title: רבא: if she was only careless, she pays for silver
steps.stepSummary: If the woman was careless and the coin was lost or stolen, she pays only for silver, since she agreed to guard only silver.
steps.simpleTranslation: If she was careless with it, she pays the value of a silver דינר. She can say to him, 'I agreed to guard silver. I never agreed to guard gold.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the second half of his rule. When the loss comes from carelessness, she pays only for what she was told the coin was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Carelessness is a failure to guard. A guard's duty covers only what she accepted. She accepted a silver coin, so her responsibility stops at silver value. This is different from step 4, where she harmed the coin directly.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two halves. If she damages it with her own hands, she pays for gold. If she is only careless, she pays for silver.

phrases.english: If she was negligent with it, she pays for a silver one,
since she can say to him:
'I took upon myself guarding silver,
I did not take upon myself guarding gold.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The second half of רבא's rule, set against the first half.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A careless watcher pays only the value she agreed to guard, which here is silver.

steps.title: רב מרדכי: רבא's rule is already clear from the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רב מרדכי tells רב אשי that the carelessness half of רבא's rule is obvious from the ברייתא about wheat covered with barley.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרדכי said to רב אשי: You teach this as רבא's own rule, but to us it is obvious from the ברייתא. Wheat covered with barley, or barley covered with wheat, is paid for only as barley. So the burner can say, 'I agreed to guard barley.' In the same way, the woman can say, 'I did not agree to guard gold.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרדכי shows that a ruling from earlier in the sugya already teaches רבא's idea. He means we did not need רבא to tell us this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, the burner pays for barley because barley is what he was shown and agreed to be responsible for. The woman was shown 'silver' and agreed to guard silver, so she pays for silver. Both cases rest on the same rule: responsibility is limited to what was accepted.
steps.whatToRemember: The wheat/barley ברייתא and רבא's gold/silver case teach the same idea. A guard is responsible only for what he agreed to watch.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that רבא's rule is not a new idea. It is an example of a broader principle about the limits of what a person takes responsibility for.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב מָרְדֳּכַי לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Mordekhai said to Rav Ashi:
You teach it as a statement of Rava;
for us, it is obvious from the baraita:
phrases.notes: He means the ברייתא already quoted in step 3.

phrases.english: Wheat covered with barley,
barley covered with wheat
he pays only
the value of barley alone.
Evidently, he can say to him:
'I took upon myself guarding barley';
here too, she can say to him:
'I did not take upon myself guarding gold.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתּוּן בִּדְרָבָא מַתְנִיתוּ לַהּ אֲנַן מִמַּתְנִיתָא פְּשִׁיטָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Links רבא's rule back to the ברייתא from step 3.
steps.raayaObject: The carelessness half of רבא's rule: she pays only for silver.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא that wheat covered with barley is paid for only as barley.

steps.title: רב heard something about רבי יהודה but forgot what
steps.stepSummary: רב says he heard a ruling connected to רבי יהודה's view but does not remember what it was.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: I heard a ruling in connection with רבי יהודה, but I don't know what it is.
steps.whatsHappening: רב says he once heard a teaching tied to רבי יהודה's opinion about fire damage, but he can't recall it. This line sets up the next step, where שמואל fills in the missing teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier steps, רבי יהודה holds that someone who starts a fire pays even for hidden items (טמון) inside the stack. רב remembers that there was an extra rule attached to this view, but not its content. On its own, this line works like an open question waiting for an answer.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב: שְׁמַעִית מִילְּתָא לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: Rav said: I heard a matter regarding Rabbi Yehuda,
phrases.notes: He means a ruling that goes along with רבי יהודה's view about hidden items burned in a fire.

phrases.english: but I do not know what it is.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: שְׁמַעִית מִילְּתָא לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, וְלָא יָדַעְנָא מַאי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the gold-coin discussion and goes back to רבי יהודה's view on hidden items in a fire.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב reports that there is a teaching attached to רבי יהודה's view, but he cannot recall what it is.

steps.title: שמואל explains: the robbery-victim rule applies to fire
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says that according to רבי יהודה, the רבנן applied תקנת נגזל to fire, so the owner may swear about the hidden items and collect.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: Does אבא really not know what he heard? According to רבי יהודה, who makes a person liable for hidden items damaged by fire, the חכמים applied the robbery-victim rule to his fire.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל supplies the teaching רב forgot. According to רבי יהודה, the owner of the burned stack may swear about what was hidden inside and then collect, just as a robbery victim does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying that the fire-starter pays for hidden items does not solve a basic problem: nobody but the owner knows what was hidden. The answer is תקנת נגזל. Just as a robbery victim may swear to what was stolen and collect it, the owner of the burned stack may swear to what was inside it.

keyTerms.meaning: Abba, the personal name of רב
the Sages' rule that a robbery victim may swear to what was taken and collect it
with his fire, meaning the one whose fire did the damage

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains how a liability for hidden items can work in practice: the victim's oath takes the place of the proof he cannot bring.

phrases.english: Shmuel said: And does Abba not know
what he heard?

phrases.aramaic: לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, דִּמְחַיֵּיב עַל נִזְקֵי טָמוּן בָּאֵשׁ –
phrases.english: According to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds one liable for damage to hidden items by fire –
they applied the robbery-victim rule to his fire.
phrases.notes: A robbery victim may swear to what was taken and then collect. Here the owner of the stack swears to what was hidden inside.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: וְלָא יָדַע אַבָּא מַאי שְׁמִיעַ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the gap left open by רב in step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to רבי יהודה, the owner of a burned stack may swear about the hidden items and collect, under תקנת נגזל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תקנת נגזל is extended to fire damage of hidden items, according to רבי יהודה.

steps.title: אמימר asks whether the rule extends to a מסור
steps.stepSummary: אמימר asks whether the רבנן also applied תקנת נגזל to a victim of a מסור.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר asks: Did they apply the robbery-victim rule to a מסור, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: אמימר asks a new question. If a מסור causes someone's property to be taken, may the victim swear about what was taken and collect?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 extended the oath-and-collect rule from robbery to fire. אמימר wants to know whether it stretches one more step, to a מסור. A מסור does not grab the property himself; he causes the authorities to take it.

keyTerms.meaning: asks a question that needs resolving
an informer who causes another's property to be seized by the government

phrases.english: Ameimar asks:

phrases.aramaic: עָשׂוּ תַּקָּנַת נִגְזָל בְּמָסוֹר, אוֹ לָא?
phrases.english: Did they apply the robbery-victim rule to an informer, or not?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 8's extension of תקנת נגזל and asks whether it reaches a new case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: May a victim of a מסור swear about what was taken and collect from the מסור?

steps.title: The question does not apply to those who reject indirect-damage liability
steps.stepSummary: Anyone who does not judge דינא דגרמי does not make a מסור pay at all, so the question cannot be asked according to that view.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who says we do not judge cases of indirect damage, don't ask, because we also don't judge cases of informers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows אמימר's question. For someone who holds that indirect damage brings no liability, a מסור pays nothing anyway, so there is nothing to swear about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מסור causes damage only indirectly, so his liability depends on דינא דגרמי. If that liability does not exist, the question of how much he pays never comes up. This removes one view from the discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: according to the one who says
the law of liability for indirect damage
you need not ask; the question does not apply

phrases.english: According to the one who says
we do not judge cases of indirect damage –
do not ask it,
because we also do not judge cases of informers;

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלִּיבָּא דְּמַאן דְּאָמַר לָא דָּיְינִינַן דִּינָא דִגְרָמֵי לָא תִּבְּעֵי לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the reach of אמימר's question from step 9.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects asking the question according to the view that does not judge דינא דגרמי.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Under that view a מסור has no liability at all, so the oath question has nothing to apply to.

steps.title: The real question: for those who judge indirect damage
steps.stepSummary: The question applies only to the view that holds people liable for דינא דגרמי: may the victim of a מסור swear and collect?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when you ask it, it is according to the one who says we judge cases of indirect damage: did they apply the robbery-victim rule to an informer, so that the victim swears and takes, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now states the question in its exact form. According to the view that a מסור does pay, may the victim set the amount with his own oath?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here it is already clear that the מסור is liable. The only open point is proof. Do we trust the victim's oath about what was taken, as we do for a robbery victim, or must he bring other evidence?

phrases.english: Rather, when you ask it,

phrases.aramaic: אַלִּיבָּא דְּמַאן דְּאָמַר דָּיְינִינַן דִּינָא דִגְרָמֵי –
phrases.english: it is according to the one who says we judge cases of indirect damage –
did they apply the robbery-victim rule to an informer,
so that he swears and takes, or not?
phrases.notes: "He" is the victim: he swears to what was taken and collects that amount from the מסור.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 10 ruled out one view, this states the question for the remaining view.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: According to the view that judges דינא דגרמי, may the victim of a מסור swear to his loss and collect?

steps.title: The question is left unresolved
steps.stepSummary: אמימר's question ends with תיקו; no answer is found.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא cannot settle אמימר's question, so it leaves it open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source decides whether the oath-and-collect rule reaches the victim of a מסור. The question is closed without a ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: let it stand; the question stays unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יהודה, the robbery-victim oath applies to hidden items destroyed by fire. Whether it applies to a מסור stays unresolved (תיקו).

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question from step 11 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: It remains undecided whether a victim of a מסור may swear and collect.

steps.title: A man kicks his friend's safe into a river
steps.stepSummary: A man kicked another person's safe into a river, and the owner claimed it held certain contents.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man kicked his friend's safe and threw it into the river. Its owner came and said: I had such-and-such inside it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells of a real case. A safe was knocked into a river, and the owner claims it held specific items. This sets up a question about whether we believe him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the hidden items in the burned stack, only the owner knows what was in the safe. The case raises the same question as before: can the owner's own claim decide the amount he collects?

keyTerms.meaning: a safe or box for valuables

phrases.english: A certain man who kicked his friend's safe,
threw it into the river.
Its owner came and said:
Such and such I had inside it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a real case that tests the same idea of trusting the victim's claim about contents nobody else saw.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Case setup: the owner of a destroyed safe claims specific contents.

steps.title: רב אשי asks what the law is in such a case
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי sits and looks into what the law is when a claimant states the contents of a destroyed safe.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי sat and examined it: in a case like this, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי asks what the ruling should be in the safe case. This sets up the discussion that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether the court believes the owner about what was inside, or whether he needs more than his own word. Steps 15–18 work this out: coins are believed, while a pearl ends as תיקו.

phrases.aramaic: יָתֵיב רַב אָשֵׁי וְקָא מְעַיֵּין בֵּיהּ:
phrases.english: Rav Ashi sat and was examining it:
In a case like this, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: יָתֵיב רַב אָשֵׁי וְקָא מְעַיֵּין בֵּיהּ: כִּי הַאי גַוְונָא מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises the legal question that the safe case in step 13 calls for.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the owner believed about the contents of the safe that was kicked into the river?

steps.title: Isn't this already answered by our משנה?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא challenges רב אחא בריה דרבא (or, in another version, רב אחא בריה דרבא challenges רב אשי): the משנה already says that someone who burns a building pays for everything inside, because people normally keep things in houses.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אחא בריה דרבא (some say רב אחא בריה דרבא said to רב אשי): Isn't this the same as our משנה? We learned: The חכמים agree with רבי יהודה that someone who sets fire to a building pays for everything inside it, because people normally keep things in houses.
steps.whatsHappening: A challenge is raised against the doubt about the safe case: why be unsure at all? The משנה already seems to answer the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה believes the owner about what was inside a burned building because people normally keep belongings in houses. People also normally keep things in a safe, so the owner of the safe should be believed too. This challenges the need to ask the question in the first place.

keyTerms.meaning: Sets fire to a large building

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא,
phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Aḥa son of Rava,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: and some say Rav Aḥa son of Rava said to Rav Ashi:
Isn't this the same as our Mishnah?
As we learned: And the Sages agree with Rabbi Yehuda
about one who sets fire to a building,
that he pays for everything inside it;

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁכֵּן דֶּרֶךְ בְּנֵי אָדָם לְהַנִּיחַ בַּבָּתִּים.
phrases.english: since people normally keep things in houses.
phrases.notes: The point is that people keep things in a safe just as they keep things in a house.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אשי's investigation from Step 14 by pointing to an existing משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's uncertainty about the contents of the kicked safe
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה already believes a claimant about items people normally keep in a building, so the same should apply to a safe.

steps.title: The question is about a pearl, not coins
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that if the man claimed there were coins, he would indeed be believed. The case in question is where he claims there was a pearl.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: If he claimed there were coins, here too he would be believed. What case are we dealing with? Where he claims there was a pearl.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי agrees with the משנה for normal items like coins. He explains that his question was about a claim of a pearl.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only covers things people normally keep in that place. Coins are normal in a safe, so the משנה's rule applies. A pearl may not be normal to keep there, so the משנה does not settle it.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי דְּקָא טָעֵין זוּזֵי –
phrases.english: He said to him: If he were claiming coins –
here too [he would be believed],
What case are we dealing with here?
Where he claims there was a pearl.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 15 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question was about any contents, which the משנה already covers.
steps.terutzMaskana: Coins are covered by the משנה; the open question is only about an unusual item like a pearl.

steps.title: Do people keep pearls in a safe?
steps.stepSummary: The real question: do people normally put pearls in a safe, so that the claimant is believed, or not?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the law? Do people put pearls in a safe, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now states the exact question. It all depends on whether keeping a pearl in a safe is normal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Following the משנה's reasoning, the claimant is believed only about what people usually keep there. So the law turns on a fact about normal behavior: is a pearl the kind of thing people store in a safe?

phrases.english: What is the law? Do people put
a pearl in a safe, or not?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: States the precise question that remains after Step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether keeping a pearl in a safe is normal, which decides whether the claimant is believed.

steps.title: The pearl question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The question about the pearl ends with תיקו; no answer is found.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא cannot decide, so the question is left open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source tells us whether people normally keep pearls in a safe. The question ends with תיקו, just like אמימר's question earlier.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question is left unanswered

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question of Step 17 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A claim of coins in a safe is believed; a claim of a pearl is left as an unresolved תיקו.
steps.whatToRemember: The claimant is believed about what people normally keep in that place. Coins in a safe are normal; whether a pearl is normal is left as תיקו.

steps.title: What about a silver goblet in a burned building?
steps.stepSummary: רב יימר asks רב אשי: if the owner of a burned building claims a silver goblet was inside, is he believed?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יימר said to רב אשי: If he claims there was a silver cup in the building, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question opens about a valuable item that not everyone owns. רב יימר wants to know if the owner is believed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A silver goblet would be kept in a house, but not every person owns one. So the question is whether the משנה's rule covers expensive items that only some people have.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יֵימַר לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Yeimar said to Rav Ashi:
If he claims a silver cup was in the building, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the safe to the burned building of the משנה, asking about a costly item.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a claim of a costly item like a silver goblet in a burned building is believed.

steps.title: It depends on who the claimant is
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that if the claimant is wealthy enough to own a silver cup, or trustworthy enough that people leave valuables with him, he swears and collects. Otherwise he is not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We look at the person. If he is wealthy and would have a silver cup, or he is trustworthy and people leave things with him, he swears and collects. If not, it is not up to him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a clear answer. Whether the claim is believed depends on whether it makes sense for this particular person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is still "is this normal?", but now it is judged for this person. A rich man would own a silver cup, and a trusted man may be holding one for someone else. For such people the claim is believable, so he takes an oath and collects; for others, his word alone is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not in his power; he is not believed

phrases.english: He said to him: We look,
phrases.notes: Some versions say "I look" (round brackets); the corrected wording is "we look" (square brackets).

phrases.english: if he is a wealthy person –
who would have a silver cup,
or if he is a trustworthy person –
with whom people leave things for safekeeping;
he swears and collects.
And if not, it is not up to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יימר's question from Step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A wealthy or trustworthy claimant swears and collects for the silver cup; anyone else is not believed.
steps.whatToRemember: For costly items, the claimant is believed with an oath only if he is wealthy enough to own it or trusted enough to be holding it for others.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that "what people normally keep" is judged by the specific person, not only by the type of item.

steps.title: How is a גזלן different from a חמסן?
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בריה דרב אויא asks רב אשי what the difference is between a גזלן and a חמסן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בריה דרב אויא said to רב אשי: What is the difference between a גזלן and a חמסן?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. The גמרא wants to define two words for people who take other people's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both words describe taking something against the owner's will. The question is what sets them apart.

keyTerms.meaning: A robber who takes by force
One who takes something against the owner's will

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַדָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אַוְיָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Adda son of Rav Avya said to Rav Ashi:
What is the difference between a gazlan and a ḥamsan?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new topic, a definition of terms, not connected to the safe or the burned building.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The difference between a גזלן and a חמסן.

steps.title: A חמסן pays; a גזלן does not
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that a חמסן pays money for what he takes, while a גזלן does not pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: A חמסן gives money; a גזלן does not give money.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי defines the two words. The difference is whether the taker pays for the item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both take against the owner's will. The חמסן forces the owner to sell and pays him, while the גזלן just takes without paying anything.
steps.confusionAlert: A חמסן is not someone who did nothing wrong because he paid. He still took the item against the owner's will; he simply paid for it.

phrases.english: He said to him: A ḥamsan gives money,
a gazlan does not give money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A חמסן pays for what he takes against the owner's will; a גזלן takes without paying.
steps.whatToRemember: Both a חמסן and a גזלן take against the owner's will; the חמסן pays, the גזלן does not.

steps.title: If he pays, why call him a robber?
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא challenges רב אשי. A person who pays should not be called a חמסן, since רב הונא rules that a forced sale is still a valid sale.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: If he gives money, you still call him a חמסן?! But didn't רב הונא say: if they hung a man up until he sold, his sale is a valid sale!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אדא pushes back on רב אשי's answer from step 22. He brings a ruling of רב הונא that seems to show a person who pays for what he takes is a legal buyer, not a robber.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי said a חמסן pays for what he takes. רב הונא holds that even a sale made under extreme pressure counts as a real sale. If so, a חמסן who pays has simply bought the item, so it seems wrong to call him any kind of robber.

keyTerms.meaning: They hung him up and he sold (he was pressured by force into selling)
His sale is a sale (it is legally valid)

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רב אדא speaking to רב אשי, reacting to the answer in step 22.

phrases.english: If he gives money,
you call him a chamsan?!
But didn't Rav Huna say:
if they hung him up and he sold,
phrases.notes: They forced the owner, even physically, until he agreed to sell.

phrases.english: his sale is a valid sale!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אשי's definition of a חמסן from step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's claim that a חמסן, who pays, is still a kind of robber.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב הונא rules that a sale made under pressure is valid. So someone who pays has legally bought the item and should not be labeled a חמסן.

steps.title: It depends on whether the seller said "I want"
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that רב הונא's valid forced sale is where the seller says "I want." The חמסן's case is where the owner never says it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This case (רב הונא's) is where the seller said "I want to sell." That case (the חמסן) is where he did not say "I want to sell."
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי settles the difficulty by splitting the two cases. One is a forced sale where the owner agreed out loud. The other is a forced taking where the owner never agreed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pressure alone does not cancel a sale if the seller ends up saying he is willing; that is רב הונא's case. A חמסן takes the item even though the owner never says he is willing. So the payment does not turn it into a real sale, and he is rightly called a חמסן.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult (the two sources do not clash)
"I want" (the seller declares he is willing)
This case... that case (splitting two situations)

steps.whatToRemember: A forced sale with payment is valid only if the seller says "רוצה אני." Without that, the taker is a חמסן even though he paid.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic rule for sales made under pressure. What decides whether the sale counts is whether the seller finally agrees.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is where he said "I want,"
phrases.notes: Here the owner himself, even while pressured, says he agrees to sell. That is רב הונא's case.

phrases.english: that is where he did not say "I want."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23 by separating the two cases.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any forced sale with payment is valid, so a paying חמסן is just a buyer.
steps.terutzMaskana: A forced sale is valid only when the seller says "רוצה אני." A חמסן takes the item without the owner ever saying that.
